How it works

A plain-language tour of the moving parts: what runs where, where the panel's data sits, what protects it, and what an update actually does.

Two programs, two kinds of machine

  • The panel — the website you log into. It holds the user list, quotas, expiry dates, settings and the audit log.
  • OVNode — an agent on every VPN server. It owns OpenVPN, the certificates and the per-user profile files.

The panel always calls the node. Nodes never call the panel — a node does not even store the panel's address — so you can move or replace the panel at any time without touching the VPN servers. Re-add them with the same address, name and API key and they carry on.

What runs where

On the panel

Two processes and one SQLite file. The web server serves requests and runs the live collector; a supervised child process runs the periodic jobs — traffic accounting, limit enforcement, backups, pruning and alerts — so a job that blocks cannot stop the panel answering. One systemd unit starts both as an unprivileged account, and the child takes an exclusive lock on the data directory so a second one cannot start and double every schedule.

There is no external database, cache or message queue to run or keep alive. A configured Telegram bot does not exist in this line: the only async noise the panel makes is the audit log, written by the jobs that produce it. The panel is reachable from the network and parses untrusted input, so a compromise of the web app should not be a compromise of the host. The panel cannot replace its own code — that needs root — so the recovery command is shell, not the web UI: sudo ovmanager update.

What the panel does instead of a cache tier:

  • One background collector polls the nodes and caches the result. Request handlers read that cache rather than fanning out to every node per request.
  • The collector backs off to OVMANAGER_LIVE_IDLE_POLL_SECONDS (default 300) when no browser has the live stream open.
  • The built index.html is cached in memory and invalidated by mtime.
  • Security headers and CSRF handling are plain middlewares, keeping the live event stream unbuffered.

On a VPN node

An OpenVPN server (systemd-managed), a small agent API on port 2083, and hooks that run at connect/disconnect time for the login limits and traffic counting. The hooks, PKI and profile files live in the node repo under OVNode. The node never calls back to the panel.

How they talk

The panel connects out to each node and calls its /sync/... endpoints. Every request carries the node's API key in a key header, and every reply is the same small envelope: 

{"success": true, "msg": "...", "data": {...}}

The panel treats a call as successful only when it gets HTTP 200 and "success": true, so the node reports business failures inside the envelope rather than as an HTTP error.

TLS is verified strictly first. A node using a self-signed certificate — the installer default — fails that check, so the panel retries once without verification and warns loudly, once per node, as a standing reminder to move that node to Let's Encrypt. TLS certificates.

Where the data lives

WhereWhat
/var/lib/ovmanagerThe panel's ovmanager.db: users, nodes, login sessions, settings and the audit log.
/opt/ovmanagerThe installed panel tree, with .env.
/etc/openvpn/server/The node's OpenVPN configuration and PKI.
/etc/openvpn/ovnode/Per-user folders, session markers, usage counters and the hooks.
/var/lib/ovnodeThe node agent's own data. Flat: one instance, one directory.

Identity: one row per user

A user is one row in the panel database with a numeric id and a display name. On the node side the panel hands out profiles keyed by that id; the node's PKI layer maps the numeric id to an OpenVPN common name so usage can be reported by username. See the OVNode project for the certificate and profile details.

Traffic accounting and limits

Every five minutes the panel asks each node for its lifetime byte totals and bills only the increase, so a restart, a disconnect or a short session cannot double-count, and a total that shrinks — a rebuilt node — bills zero rather than a negative number. The full picture, including enforcement, is in Traffic limits.

The device limit is not policed from the panel. max_logins is pushed to every node and enforced by the connect hook: 1 means a new connection takes over the old one, N rejects the N+1th, and 0 is unlimited. Session identity is the CN plus the VPN pool address, which stays stable for the life of a session — so users whose real address changes on every reconnect are still counted and limited correctly. The panel only aggregates session counts, and can disconnect a user on any node.

Security model

  • Credentials live in the database, not in .env. The owner is an ordinary row; ADMIN_USERNAME in .env only says which row is the owner. The owner password is a bcrypt hash in the database, set with ovmanager reset-password.
  • Secrets are protected by file modes. Sensitive values are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM using a key in the data directory (mode 0600); the data and backup directories are 0700 and the database, node certificates and backup copies are 0600. Treat an off-site backup as secret material and move it over an encrypted channel.
  • Secret URL path. The panel is served under a random prefix such as /dashboard/. Anything outside it gets an empty 404, so internet scanners see an empty site. It hides the panel; it is not login.
  • Database-backed sessions. A login returns an opaque random token; only its SHA-256 hash is stored. Sessions slide on activity and expire. Failed logins are rate-limited per user and per address.
  • On the node the OpenVPN management interface listens on localhost only and requires a password file. The PKI is ECDSA (prime256v1) with tls-crypt, a TLS 1.3 minimum, CRL enforcement and privilege dropping to an unprivileged runtime user. A PKI failure starts the agent in diagnostics mode instead of killing it.

Updates

The installer does not build from source. It downloads a release binary straight from GitHub Releases. sudo ovmanager update stages the new tree, health-checks it and rolls back automatically if it does not come up. An update interrupted by a reboot or power loss is recovered on the next update run. The database migrates itself on the next start. The previous tree is kept for inspection; the panel's data is restored with ovmanager restore.

On a node, ovnode update takes a verified snapshot of the identity file, the node data directory, /etc/openvpn and the API TLS files before it swaps in a release, and restores the snapshot if the new release does not come up healthy. ovnode rollback returns to the previous code tree.

Backups

ovmanager backup writes a verified .db snapshot of the panel database with older copies pruned by the keep count; the daily systemd timer runs ovmanager backup --keep 7. It can also push the newest copy offsite over SSH.

ovnode backup archives the node data and the OpenVPN PKI into root-only tarballs in /var/backups, keeping 14 by default. ovnode restore takes a safety copy before it replaces anything.
